reviews.review: Who needs ranged weapons when you have the Thunder Hammer

This is a NINE year old game as I write this, yet it was the first I came back to when I made my new gaming rig. Why is that? Isn't Space Marine kind of bare-bones? Isn't it playing it safe all the time? Well, let me explain to you why Space Marine is not just a good game, but a third-person shooter classic! 

First, unlike other third-person shooters that came out around the year of our lord 2009, Space Marine eschews the popular cover mechanic, instead pushing you to regain health by doing brutal execution moves. This pushes you [b]towards[/b] action, not some fake semblance of action where you blindfire over a three foot wall for a minute while waiting the monstrosity out.

Secondly, and way, way more important: Space Marine is really two 6\10 games who combine into a single 9\10 game. 
[list]
[*]On  one hand is the Third-Person Shooter game. It is bare-bones, nothing innovative in itself. The shooting feels sturdy and on-point, but not brilliant. This part has regenerating shields rewarding avoiding injury and not putting yourself in danger. I'd say this game has about 10 minutes of gameplay in it before it starts getting repetitive
[*]On the other hand is a Third-Person [b]Fighting[/b] game. It is also quite bare-bones, feels meaty and your moves has a distinct feel of impact when connecting with the Orks. Using execution moves you can regain health, but you can still take damage from other sources while doing them. But again, nothing beyond the ken of ordinary man. I'd say this has  another 10 minutes going for it.
[/list]

And this is where pacing comes in. So I have two games in one, both fun but with little staying power.  If Space Marine had gotten it wrong then this would have been very, very obvious to everybody and it would have been a bad game. But the makers of Space Marine didn't get the balance wrong, they got it [b]absolutely[/b] right.

Going back to the 10 minutes of gameplay, Space Marine never feels repetitive, because you're never stuck with a single game mode for ten minutes. You switch between using close combat and shooting [b]all the time[/b], rarely going more than a minute before switching. You don't need to switch weapons to do this either, you fire the gun, slam into an ork, cut another one open with the chainsword then roll away and shoot the last guy. I have described it as two separate games, but it [b]never feels[/b] like there's a disconnect in the gameplay, everything is fluid, immediate, natural and under your control. And so you never use up your ten minutes of gameplay, because the game keeps making sure you're not stuck just shooting or just fighting, you have to do both, and it keeps feeling fresh because of it.

This game is quite simply fun.
